lessons.sub: Count operations before you write code
lessons.goal: By the end you can analyse any solution's time and space complexity, recognise the Big-O classes that matter in interviews, and estimate whether a solution fits the limits before coding it.
lessons.body:
1. Big-O is about growth, not stopwatches

Big-O describes how a solution's cost grows as the input grows. An O(n) scan of 10 items and of 10 million items differs by a factor of a million; an O(n²) solution differs by a factor of a trillion. That is why interviewers care about complexity more than raw speed: hardware changes, growth does not. Always state the cost in terms of the input size n, and drop constants and lower-order terms, because at interview scale only the dominant term decides whether you pass.

2. The classes you must recognise instantly

Memorise the ladder: O(1) constant, O(log n) halving, O(n) single pass, O(n log n) good sorting, O(n²) nested loops, O(2ⁿ) brute-force subsets. A useful sense of scale: n = 10⁵ allows O(n log n) easily, O(n²) needs 10¹⁰ operations and will time out, and O(2ⁿ) dies around n = 25. When you see nested loops over the same array, think n²; when you see a problem halved each step, think log n; when you see every subset tried, think 2ⁿ.

3. Counting loops and recursion

Sequential loops add, nested loops multiply, and a loop that halves its range each time contributes log n. Recursion costs depth times work per level: a recursion tree of depth n with one call per level is O(n) time and O(n) stack space, while branching recursion like naive Fibonacci explodes to O(2ⁿ). Always count the hidden costs too: slicing a list copies it in O(n), sorting costs O(n log n), and a hash-map lookup is O(1) on average but O(n) in the worst case.

4. Space, trade-offs, and the interview habit

Time and space trade against each other constantly: a hash map buys O(1) lookups with O(n) extra memory, and sorting in place saves memory but costs O(n log n) time. In an interview, name the complexity of your brute force first, then say what you will trade to improve it. That sentence alone signals senior thinking. Before coding, check the constraints: if n ≤ 10³, O(n²) is fine; if n ≥ 10⁵, you need O(n log n) or better.

def binary_search(nums, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if nums[mid] == target:
            return mid
        if nums[mid] < target:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid - 1
    return -1

# Halves the search space each step: O(log n) time, O(1) space.
lessons.task: Solve Two Sum, Valid Anagram, Maximum Subarray, Contains Duplicate and Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock on LeetCode. For each one, write the time and space complexity of your first solution AND your optimised solution in your mistake log before you submit — no complexity note, no submit.
checks: Why is an O(n²) solution unacceptable when n = 10⁵?
It needs about 10¹⁰ operations, far beyond the roughly 10⁸ operations a typical 1–2 second limit allows. You need O(n log n) or better.
A loop runs n times and inside it you slice a list of length n. What is the total complexity?
O(n²): each slice copies n elements, so n iterations times O(n) work per iteration.
interview: Explain Big-O to a non-technical person in 30 seconds.
It describes how the work grows as the input grows. Doubling the input doubles the work for a linear solution, but quadruples it for a quadratic one — so we pick solutions whose work grows slowly.
Your solution is O(n) time and O(n) space. The interviewer asks for O(1) space. What do you do?
Look for an in-place approach: sort the input, use two pointers, or reuse the input array for bookkeeping, and state what you give up — usually time, or mutating the input.
cards: Big-O
An upper bound on how a solution's cost grows with input size n, ignoring constants and lower-order terms.
O(log n)
Cost grows with the number of times you can halve n — the signature of binary search and balanced-tree operations.
O(n log n)
The cost of efficient comparison sorting, and the target complexity for most problems with n around 10⁵.
Amortised O(1)
Average cost per operation over many operations, even if single operations occasionally cost more — like appending to a dynamic array.
Recursion depth
The maximum number of nested calls on the stack; it sets the space cost of a recursive solution.
Time-space trade-off
Using extra memory, like a hash map, to buy faster time — or the reverse. Naming the trade is half the interview answer.

lessons.sub: One pass, two indices, zero extra space
lessons.goal: By the end you can solve array problems with two pointers and sliding windows, explain when an in-place pass beats extra memory, and avoid the off-by-one errors that sink array rounds.
lessons.body:
1. Arrays are contiguous memory

An array stores elements side by side, so indexing is O(1) — the address is just base plus index times element size. The price is that inserting or deleting in the middle shifts everything after it, costing O(n). That single fact drives most array design: read-heavy, index-heavy work loves arrays, while frequent middle insertions want a linked list instead. In interviews, assume the array is the default structure and ask whether sorting it first unlocks a cheaper pattern.

2. The two-pointer pattern

Two pointers turn many O(n²) pair problems into O(n). The opposite-ends variant works on sorted input: one pointer at each end, moving inward based on whether the current sum is too small or too large. The same-direction variant has a slow pointer marking the boundary of the processed region and a fast pointer scanning ahead — the shape of every remove-duplicates problem. The recognition cue is a pair or a partition; the precondition is usually sorted input, so sorting is often step one.

3. Prefix sums and the one-pass mindset

A prefix-sum array answers any range-sum query in O(1) after one O(n) pass, and the running-sum variant answers subarray problems without storing anything extra. Kadane's algorithm is the same idea for maximum subarray: carry the best sum ending here, reset it when it goes negative. Whenever a brute force recomputes a sum or a scan from scratch inside a loop, ask what running value would make that work free.

4. Off-by-one errors and bounds

Most array failures are boundary failures: a loop that runs one step too far, a pointer that crosses its partner, or a window that never shrinks. Defend yourself with invariants: state out loud what each pointer means before the loop, and test the empty array, the single element, and the all-equal array. If your loop condition is while left < right, know exactly what equality means for your answer, and trace two tiny examples by hand before trusting it.

def two_sum_sorted(nums, target):
    left, right = 0, len(nums) - 1
    while left < right:
        total = nums[left] + nums[right]
        if total == target:
            return [left + 1, right + 1]
        if total < target:
            left += 1
        else:
            right -= 1
    return []

# Sorted input lets two pointers find the pair in O(n), O(1) space.
lessons.task: Solve Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted, Container With Most Water, 3Sum, Trapping Rain Water and Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array. For each, first write the brute force and its complexity, then the two-pointer or prefix-sum version — log both in your mistake log.
checks: When does the opposite-ends two-pointer pattern apply?
When the input is sorted and you need a pair satisfying a condition — the pointers move inward based on whether the current pair is too small or too large.
Why is Kadane's algorithm O(n) instead of O(n²)?
It carries the best subarray sum ending at the current index forward, resetting when negative, so each element is processed once instead of restarting a scan at every index.
interview: You sorted the array to use two pointers, but the problem asks for original indices. What now?
Keep the original indices alongside the values — sort pairs of (value, index) — or use a hash map, which preserves indices at the cost of O(n) extra space.
How do you avoid off-by-one errors in two-pointer code?
State the invariant for each pointer before the loop, decide what left == right means, and trace the empty, single-element and two-element cases by hand.
cards: Two pointers
Using two indices that move through an array by a rule, turning pair and partition problems from O(n²) into O(n).
Opposite ends
One pointer at each end of a sorted array, moving inward — the classic pair-sum pattern.
Prefix sum
A running total that answers any range sum in O(1) after one O(n) preprocessing pass.
Kadane's algorithm
Maximum subarray in O(n): keep the best sum ending here, reset to zero when it goes negative.
In-place
Solving without extra arrays, usually with two pointers — O(1) extra space, but it mutates the input.
Off-by-one
A boundary error where a loop runs one step too many or too few; the most common array bug in interviews.

lessons.sub: Hash maps turn O(n²) into O(n)
lessons.goal: By the end you can use frequency maps and sliding windows to solve string problems in linear time, and explain the cost of string immutability when you build results.
lessons.body:
1. Strings are immutable arrays of characters

In most languages a string cannot be changed in place: every concatenation builds a new string, so building a result with += inside a loop costs O(n²). The fix is to collect pieces in a list and join them once, which is O(n). The same immutability makes strings hashable and safe as dictionary keys, which is exactly why the hashing patterns in this lesson work. Treat a string as an array of characters with a few extra operations, and its behaviour stops being surprising.

2. Hashing: the frequency-map habit

A hash map stores key-value pairs with average O(1) lookup, and the frequency map is its most-used interview form: one pass to count characters or numbers, then answer any question about duplicates, anagrams or complements from the counts. Two Sum is the canonical example — for each number, check whether its complement is already in the map. The habit to build is asking, whenever you see a nested loop, whether a map could remember what the inner loop is searching for.

3. Anagrams, grouping, and the two-sum trick

Two strings are anagrams when their character counts match, so the signature of a string — its sorted form or its 26-count tuple — becomes a hash-map key that groups anagrams together. The same complement trick from Two Sum generalises: any problem asking whether a pair or group satisfies a condition is a candidate for one pass plus a map. Watch the key choice, though: using a sorted string as a key costs O(k log k) per word, while a count tuple is O(k).

4. Sliding window on strings

When a problem asks for the longest or smallest substring satisfying a condition, the window is the pattern: a right pointer expands, a left pointer shrinks when the condition breaks, and a map tracks what is inside. Longest substring without repeats is the template — expand until a duplicate appears, then move left past the previous occurrence. The window never moves backwards, so the whole scan is O(n), and the only state you maintain is the map and the best answer seen.

def longest_unique(s):
    seen = {}
    left = best = 0
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        if ch in seen and seen[ch] >= left:
            left = seen[ch] + 1
        seen[ch] = right
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best

# Sliding window + last-seen map: O(n) time, O(1) space for ASCII.
lessons.task: Solve Valid Anagram, Group Anagrams, Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters, Longest Repeating Character Replacement and Minimum Window Substring. For each failed or 45+ minute attempt, log the pattern, what went wrong, and a re-solve date 3 days out.
checks: Why is building a string with += in a loop O(n²)?
Strings are immutable, so each += copies the whole string built so far. Collect pieces in a list and join once for O(n).
In the sliding-window template, why does the left pointer never move backwards?
The window only grows or slides forward, so each character enters and leaves the window once — that is what makes the scan O(n).
interview: How would you check whether two strings are anagrams in O(n)?

Count characters of the first string in a frequency map, subtract the second string's counts, and check every count is zero — or compare 26-length count arrays. Sorting also works but costs O(n log n).
When is a hash map the wrong tool?
When order matters, when you need the minimum or maximum key, or when memory is tight — a sorted structure or two pointers may fit better despite the O(log n) lookup.
cards: Frequency map
A hash map counting how often each key appears — the core tool for anagram, duplicate and complement problems.
Hash map
A key-value store with average O(1) insert and lookup; collisions can degrade it to O(n) in the worst case.
Sliding window
Two pointers marking a substring that grows and shrinks in one pass, giving O(n) solutions for substring problems.
Anagram signature
A canonical key for a string — sorted letters or a 26-count tuple — shared by all its anagrams.
String immutability
Strings cannot be changed in place; every edit creates a new string, so repeated concatenation is O(n²).
Complement trick
For each value x, look up target − x in a map instead of scanning for a partner — the heart of Two Sum.

lessons.sub: Trust the recursion — define the base case, then the choice
lessons.goal: By the end you can write recursive solutions with correct base cases, implement backtracking with choose-explore-undo, and estimate the size of a decision tree before coding it.
lessons.body:
1. Recursion is a call stack, not magic

A recursive function solves a smaller version of the same problem and trusts the result. Two things must be right: the base case, which stops the recursion, and the progress step, which guarantees the input shrinks toward it. Every call frame sits on the stack, so depth n costs O(n) space, and a missing base case is an infinite recursion that ends in a stack overflow. When you are stuck, write the base case first, then the recursive step for the smallest non-trivial input, and trace it by hand.

2. Backtracking: choose, explore, undo

Backtracking explores a decision tree depth-first: pick a candidate, recurse, then undo the pick so the next branch starts clean. That undo step is the whole pattern — forgetting it is the most common backtracking bug, and it produces answers polluted by earlier choices. The template is identical across subsets, permutations, combinations and word search; only the choice set and the validity check change. If you can write one backtracking solution cleanly, you can write them all.

3. The decision-tree mental model

Before coding, draw the tree: each level is one decision, each path from root to leaf is one candidate answer. Subsets branch include-or-exclude at each element, giving 2ⁿ leaves; permutations branch over the remaining elements, giving n! leaves. Counting the leaves first tells you the complexity and whether pruning is needed. This model also explains why backtracking is exponential by nature — you are enumerating candidates, not computing a formula.

4. Pruning and the complexity check

Pruning cuts branches that cannot lead to a valid answer, using a constraint check before recursing — for example, skipping duplicate values in Combination Sum by sorting first and ignoring repeats. Pruning never changes the worst case, but it decides whether a solution passes in practice. Always state the worst-case complexity honestly: O(2ⁿ) for subsets, O(n!) for permutations. If the constraints allow that, backtracking is the right tool; if not, you need memoisation or DP.

def subsets(nums):
    result, path = [], []
    def backtrack(i):
        if i == len(nums):
            result.append(path[:])
            return
        path.append(nums[i])
        backtrack(i + 1)
        path.pop()
        backtrack(i + 1)
    backtrack(0)
    return result

# Each element: include or exclude. 2^n leaves, O(n * 2^n) total work.
lessons.task: Solve Subsets, Permutations, Combination Sum, Generate Parentheses and Word Search. For each, draw the decision tree for a 3-element input on paper first, then code — and log any solution where you forgot the undo step.
checks: What are the two things a recursive function must get right?
A base case that stops the recursion, and a progress step that shrinks the input toward the base case on every call.
Why is the undo step essential in backtracking?
Each branch must start from the same state. Without undoing the choice, later branches inherit earlier picks and produce wrong answers.
interview: How do you decide between recursion and iteration?

Recursion fits problems with a natural self-similar structure — trees, decision trees, divide and conquer. Iteration fits flat loops and avoids stack-depth limits; deep recursion can overflow the stack.
Your backtracking solution is too slow. What do you try first?
Prune invalid branches earlier, memoise repeated subproblems if they overlap, and check whether the problem has optimal substructure that allows DP instead of enumeration.
cards: Base case
The smallest input a recursive function answers directly, without another recursive call — it stops the recursion.
Call stack
The stack of active function calls; recursion depth equals stack depth, and each frame costs memory.
Backtracking
Depth-first search over choices with an undo step: choose, explore, then remove the choice before the next branch.
Decision tree
A tree where each level is one choice and each root-to-leaf path is one candidate answer; its leaf count is the complexity.
Pruning
Skipping branches that cannot lead to a valid answer, checked before recursing deeper.
Stack overflow
Exhausting the call stack, usually from a missing base case or recursion deeper than the stack allows.

lessons.sub: Pointers, not indexes — draw the arrows first
lessons.goal: By the end you can manipulate linked lists with dummy nodes and fast/slow pointers, reverse a list in place, and explain exactly where each pointer points at every step.
lessons.body:
1. Nodes and pointers: why lists exist

A linked list is a chain of nodes, each holding a value and a pointer to the next node. Unlike an array, a list can grow and shrink by rewiring one pointer in O(1), but reaching the tenth node means walking nine pointers — random access is O(n). That trade-off is the whole story: lists win when you insert and delete at known positions, arrays win when you index. In interviews the list is rarely the end goal; it is the stage where pointer discipline is tested.

2. The dummy node trick

Most linked-list bugs live at the head: deleting the first node, merging from an empty list, or building a new list from scratch all need special cases. A dummy node sitting before the real head removes them — you always have a previous node, and the answer is dummy.next at the end. This one trick simplifies merge, remove-nth, and partition problems so much that reaching for it should be automatic. When a problem builds or rewrites a list, start with a dummy.

3. Fast and slow pointers

Two pointers moving at different speeds through a list detect structure that one pointer cannot see. A fast pointer moving two steps per slow pointer's one catches up exactly when there is a cycle, and when the fast pointer reaches the end, the slow pointer sits at the middle. The same idea finds the nth node from the end: advance fast by n, then move both together. The pattern is always the same — create a gap or a speed difference, then let the pointers meet.

4. Reversal: the interview rite of passage

Reversing a list in place is the most-asked linked-list operation because it tests whether you can hold three pointers in your head: previous, current, and next. The loop saves next, flips current.next to previous, then advances both — and the classic bug is losing next before the flip, which severs the list. Draw the arrows on paper before you type a line. If you can reverse a list cold, you can do almost any pointer surgery an interview will ask for.

def reverse_list(head):
    prev, curr = None, head
    while curr:
        nxt = curr.next
        curr.next = prev
        prev = curr
        curr = nxt
    return prev

# Three pointers, one flip per step: O(n) time, O(1) space.
lessons.task: Solve Reverse Linked List, Merge Two Sorted Lists, Linked List Cycle, Remove Nth Node From End of List and Reorder List. Draw the pointer state on paper for every problem before coding, and log any attempt where you lost a node by overwriting a pointer too early.
checks: Why does a dummy node simplify linked-list code?
It guarantees a previous node always exists, so head deletion, empty-list merges and building a new list need no special case — the answer is dummy.next.
How do fast and slow pointers detect a cycle?
The fast pointer moves two steps per slow step, so if there is a cycle it must eventually lap the slow pointer and meet it; on an acyclic list it reaches the end.
interview: Reverse a linked list — and narrate what each pointer holds at each step.
Keep prev, curr and next. Save next, point curr.next at prev, advance prev to curr and curr to next. The list is never lost because next is saved before the flip.
Why would you choose a linked list over an array?
When insertions and deletions at known positions dominate, since rewiring one pointer is O(1) while an array shifts O(n) elements — at the cost of O(n) random access.
cards: Node
One element of a linked list: a value plus a pointer to the next node (and prev, in a doubly linked list).
Dummy node
A throwaway node placed before the head so edge cases at the head disappear; the answer is dummy.next.
Fast and slow pointers
Two pointers moving at different speeds — used to find cycles, middles, and the nth node from the end.
Pointer surgery
Rewiring next pointers to insert, delete or reverse nodes without copying values.
Cycle detection
Floyd's algorithm: fast laps slow inside a cycle, so a meeting proves a cycle exists in O(n) time, O(1) space.
In-place reversal
Flipping next pointers one node at a time with three pointers, using O(1) extra space.

lessons.sub: LIFO and FIFO — the order is the algorithm
lessons.goal: By the end you can recognise when a problem is a stack problem, use monotonic stacks for next-greater problems, and implement stacks and queues from each other.
lessons.body:
1. Stack: undo, matching, and nesting

A stack is last-in-first-out: push adds to the top, pop removes from the top, and peek reads it. That order is exactly what nested structures need — an opening bracket waits on the stack until its closing bracket arrives, and an undo history replays in reverse. Valid Parentheses is the purest form: push opens, match-and-pop closes, and anything left over means imbalance. Whenever a problem involves nesting, reversal, or most-recent-first processing, reach for the stack before anything else.

2. The monotonic stack pattern

A monotonic stack keeps its elements in increasing or decreasing order, popping anything that breaks the order. It answers next-greater-element questions in O(n): each element is pushed once and popped once, and the pop reveals the next greater element for everything removed. Daily Temperatures is the same shape — the stack holds indices waiting for a warmer day. The recognition cue is a problem asking for the next element that is bigger or smaller than the current one.

3. Queues and breadth-first thinking

A queue is first-in-first-out: enqueue at the back, dequeue from the front. It is the order of fairness — tasks processed in arrival order — and the engine of breadth-first search, which visits nodes level by level. A double-ended queue, or deque, allows both ends and powers sliding-window maximum, where the deque holds candidates in decreasing order. Knowing which end each operation touches is the difference between a queue and a stack.

4. Designing with stacks and queues

Min Stack shows how to extend a stack: store each value alongside the minimum so far, and getMin becomes O(1). Implementing a queue with two stacks shows the deeper idea — one stack for input, one for output, with a transfer that reverses order exactly once per element, giving amortised O(1) operations. Interviewers love these design problems because they test whether you understand the order, not just the API.

def is_valid(s):
    stack = []
    pairs = {')': '(', ']': '[', '}': '{'}
    for ch in s:
        if ch in '([{':
            stack.append(ch)
        elif not stack or stack.pop() != pairs[ch]:
            return False
    return not stack

# Push opens, match-and-pop closes: O(n) time, O(n) space.
lessons.task: Solve Valid Parentheses, Min Stack, Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation, Daily Temperatures and Implement Queue using Stacks. For Daily Temperatures, first write the O(n²) brute force, then the monotonic-stack version, and compare both in your log.
checks: Why does Valid Parentheses need a stack rather than just counting brackets?
Counting cannot check order or type — '([)]' has balanced counts but wrong nesting. A stack matches each closer with the most recent opener.
In a monotonic stack, why is each element pushed and popped at most once?
Once popped, an element never returns, so total pushes and pops across the whole run are O(n) — that is why the algorithm is linear.
interview: Design a stack that returns the minimum in O(1).
Store each pushed value together with the minimum so far, or keep a parallel min-stack. getMin then reads the top of the min-stack in O(1).
How do you implement a queue using two stacks?
Push into the input stack; to dequeue, move everything to the output stack if it is empty, which reverses order. Each element moves at most twice, so operations are amortised O(1).
cards: Stack (LIFO)
Last-in-first-out: push and pop happen at the same end — the top. Used for nesting, undo and reversal.
Queue (FIFO)
First-in-first-out: enqueue at the back, dequeue from the front. Used for fair ordering and breadth-first search.
Monotonic stack
A stack kept in increasing or decreasing order by popping violators — solves next-greater-element problems in O(n).
Deque
Double-ended queue: insert and remove at both ends in O(1). Powers sliding-window maximum.
Amortised O(1)
Average cost per operation over a sequence, even when single operations occasionally cost more — like transferring between two stacks.
Min Stack
A stack that also tracks the minimum so far, giving getMin in O(1) by storing the running minimum with each push.

lessons.sub: Sorted input is a superpower — halve the search space
lessons.goal: By the end you can write a correct binary search from its invariant, apply it to rotated arrays and to search-the-answer problems, and choose the right sort for the job.
lessons.body:
1. Sorting first is often the whole solution

Comparison sorting costs O(n log n), and paying it once can unlock linear patterns everywhere else: two pointers need sorted input, duplicates become adjacent, and binary search becomes possible. That is why so many interview solutions start with a sort — the O(n log n) is cheap compared with the O(n²) it replaces. Know your sorts: merge sort is stable and always O(n log n), quicksort is fast in practice but O(n²) worst case, and counting sort is O(n + k) when values are bounded.

2. The binary search invariant

Binary search works on any sorted input, and the correct way to write it is from its invariant: the answer, if it exists, is always inside [lo, hi]. Each step compares the middle element and discards the half that cannot contain the answer, halving the range until lo passes hi. The classic bugs — infinite loops and missed elements — all come from updating lo and hi inconsistently with the invariant. Write the invariant as a comment, use lo = mid + 1 and hi = mid − 1, and the loop terminates.

3. Binary search on the answer

The most powerful form of binary search does not search an array at all: it searches a range of possible answers. In Koko Eating Bananas, the answer is a speed between 1 and the maximum pile; a feasibility check — can Koko finish at this speed — is monotonic, so binary search finds the smallest feasible speed. The recognition cue is a question asking for the minimum or maximum value satisfying a yes-or-no condition that flips once as the value grows.

4. Rotated arrays and edge cases

A rotated sorted array is still searchable in O(log n) because one half is always sorted: compare the middle element with the ends to find which half is ordered, then check whether the target lies inside it. The same invariant thinking applies, but the branch logic doubles, so tracing a three-element example is essential. Always test the unrotated case, the single-element case, and the target at both ends — these are where rotated-array solutions silently fail.

def binary_search(nums, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if nums[mid] == target:
            return mid
        if nums[mid] < target:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid - 1
    return -1

# Invariant: the target, if present, is in [lo, hi]. O(log n) time.
lessons.task: Solve Binary Search, Search in Rotated Sorted Array, Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array, Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted Array and Koko Eating Bananas. Write the loop invariant as a comment in each solution before you run it.
checks: What is the loop invariant of binary search, and why does it prevent infinite loops?
The target, if present, is always within [lo, hi]. Each step shrinks that range by at least half, so the loop must terminate.
When can you binary-search an answer that is not in any array?
When the question asks for a minimum or maximum value and the feasibility check is monotonic — feasible answers stay feasible as the value grows, so the boundary is searchable.
interview: Why is merge sort stable and quicksort not, and when does it matter?
Merge sort preserves the order of equal elements; quicksort's swaps do not. Stability matters when sorting by one key after another, like sorting records by date then by name.
How do you find the minimum in a rotated sorted array in O(log n)?
Compare mid with the right end: if nums[mid] is greater, the minimum is in the right half; otherwise it is in the left half including mid. Repeat until one element remains.
cards: Binary search
Repeatedly halving a sorted range using the invariant that the target, if present, lies inside [lo, hi] — O(log n).
Loop invariant
A statement that stays true before every iteration; the anchor that makes binary search correct and its loop terminate.
Binary search on answer
Searching a range of candidate answers with a monotonic feasibility check, instead of searching an array.
Stable sort
A sort that keeps equal elements in their original relative order — merge sort is stable, quicksort is not.
Counting sort
Sorting by counting frequencies when values are bounded: O(n + k) time, but needs O(k) extra space.
Rotated sorted array
A sorted array cut and swapped; one half is always sorted, which keeps binary search at O(log n).

lessons.goal: By the end you can implement tree traversals recursively and iteratively, use the BST property to search in O(log n), and solve depth, diameter and ancestor problems with one recursive pattern.
lessons.body:
1. Trees are recursive data

A tree is a node with a value and pointers to children; a binary tree has at most two. The key insight is that every subtree is itself a tree, so every tree problem is a recursion problem: solve it for the left and right children, combine the results at the current node. Depth is one plus the deeper child's depth, and the size is one plus both children's sizes. Once you see the subtree structure, the recursion writes itself.

2. Traversals: four orders, one idea

Traversal order is just when you visit the node relative to its children: preorder visits the node first, inorder between the children, postorder last, and level order visits breadth-first with a queue. Inorder on a binary search tree yields the values sorted — that single fact powers validation, kth-smallest and recovery problems. Iterative traversals use an explicit stack and mirror the recursion exactly; learn the recursive form first, then the iterative one for interviews that demand it.

3. The BST property is a search superpower

In a binary search tree, every left descendant is smaller and every right descendant is larger than the node. That ordering turns search into a walk: go left if the target is smaller, right if larger, and you reach any node in O(h) time — O(log n) when the tree is balanced. It also makes validation a range problem: pass down a (low, high) window and check each node lies inside it. A tree that violates the property at any node is not a BST, however sorted its inorder looks locally.

4. Depth, diameter, and lowest common ancestors

Most tree interview problems are one recursive helper returning information upward. Diameter is the longest path through a node, computed from the depths of its children, with the answer tracked globally. Lowest common ancestor in a BST is a walk: if both targets are smaller, go left; if both larger, go right; otherwise this node is the split point. The pattern is always the same — define what the helper returns, handle the null base case, and combine children.

def invert(root):
    if not root:
        return None
    root.left, root.right = invert(root.right), invert(root.left)
    return root

# Swap children at every node, bottom-up: O(n) time, O(h) stack space.
lessons.task: Solve Invert Binary Tree, Maximum Depth of Binary Tree, Diameter of Binary Tree, Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree and Validate Binary Search Tree. For Validate BST, implement the range-based version, not the inorder-list version.
checks: Why does inorder traversal of a BST give sorted values?
Inorder visits left subtree, then node, then right subtree — and the BST property guarantees left values are smaller and right values larger, so the visit order is ascending.
How is tree diameter different from tree height?
Height is the longest downward path from a node; diameter is the longest path between any two nodes, which may pass through a node via both its children.
interview: How do you validate a BST in one pass?
Recurse with a (low, high) range: each node must lie strictly inside it, and children get narrowed ranges — left child capped by the node, right child floored by it.
When is a BST search O(n) instead of O(log n)?
When the tree is unbalanced, like a chain from inserting sorted values — height becomes n. A balanced tree, or a self-balancing one, keeps height at log n.
cards: Binary tree
A tree where each node has at most a left and a right child; every subtree is itself a tree.
BST property
Left descendants are smaller and right descendants larger than the node — this makes search O(h).
Inorder traversal
Left, node, right — visits a BST's values in ascending sorted order.
Height vs depth
Height is the longest downward path from a node; depth is the distance from the root to the node.
Diameter
The longest path between any two nodes in a tree, which may pass through a node via both children.
Lowest common ancestor
The deepest node that is an ancestor of both targets — in a BST it is the first node where the targets split.

lessons.sub: The top-k pattern — keep only what matters
lessons.goal: By the end you can use min-heaps and max-heaps for top-k, merge and scheduling problems, and explain exactly when a heap beats a full sort.
lessons.body:
1. A heap is a partial order, not a sorted list

A heap is a binary tree where every parent is smaller than its children (min-heap) or larger (max-heap), stored compactly in an array. Only the top element is guaranteed — the rest is unordered. That partial order is the point: inserting and removing the top both cost O(log n), while building a heap from n elements costs O(n). If a problem only ever needs the smallest or largest element, a heap gives it without paying for a full sort.

2. The top-k pattern

Top-k problems are the heap's home ground. To find the k largest elements, keep a min-heap of size k: push each element, and whenever the heap exceeds k, pop the smallest. At the end the heap holds exactly the k largest, in O(n log k) time and O(k) space. The same shape solves Top K Frequent Elements — count frequencies first, then heap by count — and K Closest Points, where the heap is ordered by distance. The cue is the word top or closest combined with a large n.

3. Merging and scheduling with heaps

When several sorted streams must merge, a heap holding one current element from each stream always yields the next smallest in O(log k) per element — the engine of Merge K Sorted Lists. Scheduling problems use the same idea: always process the available job with the earliest deadline or shortest duration, which a heap supplies on demand. Whenever the next step is always the extreme of a changing set, a heap is the structure doing the choosing.

4. Heap versus sort: choosing the tool

Sorting costs O(n log n) once and then answers every order question in O(1); a heap costs O(n log k) for top-k and O(log n) per update, but shines when data arrives over time or k is much smaller than n. For a stream where the kth largest is asked repeatedly, a min-heap of size k answers in O(1) after each insertion. The interview move is to name both options and their costs, then pick by whether the data is static or streaming and whether k is small.

import heapq

def kth_largest(nums, k):
    heap = []
    for x in nums:
        heapq.heappush(heap, x)
        if len(heap) > k:
            heapq.heappop(heap)
    return heap[0]

# Min-heap of size k keeps only the k largest: O(n log k) time.
lessons.task: Solve Kth Largest Element in an Array, Top K Frequent Elements, Last Stone Weight, K Closest Points to Origin and Find Median from Data Stream. For Find Median, implement the two-heap version and trace it on paper for the stream 1, 5, 2.
checks: Why is building a heap O(n) instead of O(n log n)?
Most nodes sit near the leaves with tiny sift-down distances; summing the work over all levels gives O(n), not n times log n.
Why does the top-k pattern use a min-heap to find the k largest?
A min-heap of size k keeps the smallest of the k largest on top, so each new element is compared against exactly the threshold it must beat.
interview: How do you find the median of a streaming sequence?
Keep a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, balanced so their sizes differ by at most one. The median is a top element or the average of both.
When is a heap worse than just sorting?
When you need the fully sorted order, or when all elements are static and queried many times — a one-time O(n log n) sort then answers everything in O(1).
cards: Min-heap
A heap where every parent is smaller than its children, so the minimum is always on top; insert and pop cost O(log n).
Max-heap
A heap where every parent is larger than its children, so the maximum is always on top.
Top-k pattern
Keep a heap of size k while scanning: push each element, pop the extreme when the heap overflows — O(n log k).
Heapify
Building a heap from an array in O(n) by sifting down from the last parent upward.
Two-heap median
A max-heap for the lower half plus a min-heap for the upper half, kept balanced, yields the running median in O(log n) per insert.
Priority queue
A queue that always dequeues the highest-priority element first, usually implemented with a heap.

lessons.sub: Nodes, edges, visited set — every graph problem is a traversal
lessons.goal: By the end you can model a problem as a graph, choose BFS or DFS deliberately, and solve islands, cloning, course-schedule and multi-source problems with a visited set.
lessons.body:
1. Modelling: everything is a graph if you look right

A graph is nodes connected by edges, and the first skill is recognising one: grid cells are nodes with four neighbours, courses are nodes with prerequisite edges, words are nodes linked by one-letter changes. The standard representation is an adjacency list — a map from each node to its neighbours — because it is O(V + E) in space and enumerates neighbours fast. Before coding any graph problem, write down what the nodes are, what the edges are, and whether edges are directed.

2. DFS versus BFS: depth or breadth

Depth-first search dives down one path before backtracking, using a stack or recursion; breadth-first search visits level by level using a queue. DFS is natural for exploring all paths, detecting cycles, and topological sorting. BFS is the tool when distance matters — it finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph because it reaches nodes in order of increasing distance. The algorithm is the same shape either way: pop a node, mark it visited, push its unvisited neighbours.

3. The visited set: the one bug that loops forever

Graphs have cycles, so a traversal without a visited set revisits nodes forever. Mark a node visited when you enqueue it, not when you dequeue it — marking late lets the same node enter the queue many times, which is the most common BFS bug. The visited set is also the answer in many problems: in Number of Islands, each unvisited land cell starts a new island, and the flood fill marks the whole island visited. If your graph code hangs, the visited set is the first suspect.

4. Classic patterns: islands, topo sort, multi-source BFS

Three patterns cover most graph interviews. Connected components: count the flood fills from unvisited nodes. Topological sort: order nodes so prerequisites come first, using DFS finishing times or Kahn's indegree algorithm — and a cycle means no valid order exists, which is the whole Course Schedule problem. Multi-source BFS: enqueue all sources at once, as in Rotting Oranges, and the level number is the minutes elapsed. Learn these three and most graph problems become variations.

from collections import deque

def bfs(grid, sr, sc):
    q = deque([(sr, sc)])
    grid[sr][sc] = '0'
    while q:
        r, c = q.popleft()
        for dr, dc in [(1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)]:
            nr, nc = r + dr, c + dc
            if 0 <= nr < len(grid) and 0 <= nc < len(grid[0]):
                if grid[nr][nc] == '1':
                    grid[nr][nc] = '0'
                    q.append((nr, nc))

# Flood fill from one island cell: O(cells) time, O(cells) queue space.
lessons.task: Solve Number of Islands, Clone Graph, Course Schedule, Pacific Atlantic Water Flow and Rotting Oranges. For Course Schedule, implement both the DFS cycle check and Kahn's algorithm and note which one you find easier to reproduce cold.
checks: Why mark a node visited when you enqueue it, not when you dequeue it?
Marking late lets the same node be enqueued many times by different neighbours, blowing up the queue and the work; marking at enqueue time guarantees one entry per node.
Why does BFS find the shortest path in an unweighted graph?
It visits nodes in order of increasing distance from the source, so the first time a node is reached is via the shortest possible path.
interview: How do you detect a cycle in a directed graph?
DFS with three states — unvisited, visiting, done. Reaching a node in the visiting state means a back edge, hence a cycle. A plain visited set is not enough for directed graphs.
When would you choose DFS over BFS?
When exploring all paths, detecting cycles, doing topological sort, or when memory matters — DFS uses O(h) stack space versus BFS's O(w) queue, which can be much larger.
cards: Adjacency list
A map from each node to its neighbours — the standard graph representation, O(V + E) in space.
BFS
Breadth-first search with a queue: visits level by level, finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs.
DFS
Depth-first search with a stack or recursion: dives down one path first; natural for cycles and topo sort.
Visited set
The record of nodes already processed; without it, cycles make a traversal loop forever.
Topological sort
An ordering of nodes so every prerequisite comes before its dependent; impossible when the graph has a cycle.
Multi-source BFS
Starting BFS from all sources at once, so the level number measures distance from the nearest source.

lessons.sub: States, choices, recurrence — DP is recursion with memory
lessons.goal: By the end you can recognise DP problems, define state and recurrence in words before coding, and convert a memoised recursion into a bottom-up table.
lessons.body:
1. Recognising DP: overlapping subproblems, optimal substructure

DP applies when a problem breaks into subproblems that repeat and the optimal answer is built from optimal answers to those subproblems. Fibonacci repeats fib(3) many times; Climbing Stairs reuses the ways to reach each step; Coin Change reuses the best answer for every smaller amount. The test is to draw the recursion tree and look for repeated nodes. If the same subproblem appears twice, memoisation will help; if the optimal answer needs optimal sub-answers, DP is the right frame.

2. The five-step method

Never code DP by feel. First, define the state in words — what dp[i] means. Second, list the choices at that state. Third, write the recurrence: dp[i] in terms of smaller states. Fourth, set the base cases. Fifth, decide the order to fill the table. Climbing Stairs is the template: dp[i] is the ways to reach step i, the choices are one or two steps, so dp[i] = dp[i−1] + dp[i−2], with dp[0] = dp[1] = 1. Saying the state aloud before coding is what separates a DP solution from a lucky guess.

3. Memoisation versus tabulation

Memoisation is top-down: write the natural recursion, cache each result, and let the call stack drive the order. Tabulation is bottom-up: fill a table in increasing order, no recursion involved. Memoisation is faster to write and only computes needed states; tabulation avoids stack limits and usually compresses space — Climbing Stairs needs only the previous two values, not the whole table. In interviews, start with memoisation to get the recurrence right, then convert to tabulation if space matters.

4. The classic pattern families

Most DP problems fall into a few families. One-dimensional DP: climbing stairs, house robber, coin change. Grid DP: unique paths, minimum path sum. Subsequence DP: longest increasing subsequence, longest common subsequence, edit distance. Knapsack DP: partition a set under a sum constraint. Each family has one canonical problem; learn it deeply and the rest are variations in state and choice. When stuck on a new DP problem, ask which family it resembles and what its state would be.

def climb_stairs(n):
    if n <= 1:
        return 1
    prev2, prev1 = 1, 1
    for _ in range(2, n + 1):
        prev2, prev1 = prev1, prev1 + prev2
    return prev1

# dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2]; two variables compress the table to O(1) space.
lessons.task: Solve Climbing Stairs, House Robber, Coin Change, Longest Increasing Subsequence and Word Break. For each, write the state definition and recurrence in your mistake log in words before coding — if you cannot state them, do not code yet.
checks: What two properties must a problem have for DP to apply?
Overlapping subproblems — the same subproblem recurs — and optimal substructure — the optimal answer is built from optimal answers to subproblems.
Why can Climbing Stairs run in O(1) space?
Each state depends only on the previous two, so the full table is unnecessary — two variables carry everything forward.
interview: How do you approach a DP problem you have never seen?
Define the state in words, list the choices, write the recurrence, set base cases, then code memoised recursion first and convert to tabulation only if needed.
What is the difference between memoisation and tabulation?
Memoisation is top-down recursion with a cache; tabulation is bottom-up table filling. Same recurrence, different order — tabulation avoids recursion depth and usually compresses space.
cards: State
The parameters that fully describe a subproblem, e.g. dp[i] = ways to reach step i — the heart of any DP solution.
Recurrence
The formula expressing a state in terms of smaller states, e.g. dp[i] = dp[i−1] + dp[i−2].
Memoisation
Top-down DP: cache recursive results so each subproblem is computed once.
Tabulation
Bottom-up DP: fill a table in increasing order, usually with less space and no recursion.
Optimal substructure
The property that an optimal solution is built from optimal solutions to its subproblems.
Space compression
Shrinking a DP table to the few previous values the recurrence actually reads, e.g. two variables instead of an array.

lessons.t: Interview Simulation — Patterns, Mock Rounds & Mistake Log
lessons.sub: Talk, code, test — under the clock
lessons.goal: By the end you can run a full 45-minute mock interview round, diagnose your own failures with a mistake log, and walk into a Summer 2027 internship interview with a practiced pattern-first routine.
lessons.body:
1. The 45-minute anatomy of an interview round

A real round has a rhythm: five minutes clarifying the problem and confirming constraints, ten minutes on a brute force with its complexity, fifteen minutes optimising to the target pattern, ten minutes coding cleanly, and five minutes testing. The most common failure is coding in the first five minutes — it skips the thinking the interviewer is actually grading. Practice the rhythm with a timer, not just the problems. If you cannot state the brute force and its complexity before coding, you are not ready to code.

2. Thinking aloud and the pattern-first reflex

Interviewers grade your thinking, not just your code, so narrate the recognition step: what pattern does this resemble, and why? Pair sums mean two pointers or a hash map; substrings mean sliding window; trees mean recursion; shortest paths mean BFS; optimisation over choices means DP. Build the reflex by naming the pattern before writing a line — in practice and in mocks. When you are stuck, say so out loud and name what you have tried; silence reads as giving up, while a stated dead end reads as problem-solving.

3. The mistake log and spaced re-solve

Every failed or 45-plus-minute problem goes in the log with three lines: the pattern, what went wrong, and a re-solve date. Re-solve after 3 days, then after 7 days, without looking at the old solution — if you cannot reproduce it, the pattern is not learned and the cycle repeats. The log is also your revision list for the final week: problems you failed twice are the ones most likely to appear in some form, and re-solving them cold is the highest-value revision there is.

4. Contests, mocks, and the final two weeks

Do the LeetCode Weekly Contest every Sunday: four problems under real time pressure, with no pausing and no editorials until the timer ends. Pair it with one full mock per week — a friend or a recorded self-interview, 45 minutes, talking aloud. In the final two weeks, stop learning new patterns; re-solve your mistake log, redo the core five per pattern, and rest the day before the interview. One rest day per week throughout the plan is not laziness — it is when the patterns consolidate.

def two_sum(nums, target):
    seen = {}
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        need = target - x
        if need in seen:
            return [seen[need], i]
        seen[x] = i
    return []

assert two_sum([2, 7, 11, 15], 9) == [0, 1]
assert two_sum([3, 3], 6) == [0, 1]

# Brute force O(n^2) -> hash map O(n). Test before you call it done.
lessons.task: Run a full mock week: one unseen Medium per pattern — Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters (sliding window), Container With Most Water (two pointers), Number of Islands (BFS), Coin Change (DP) and LRU Cache (design) — 45 minutes each, talking aloud, timed. Log every failure with pattern, cause and a 3-day re-solve date, and do the Sunday LeetCode Weekly Contest under real conditions.
checks: What is the five-part structure of a 45-minute interview round?
Clarify (5 min), brute force with complexity (10), optimise to the pattern (15), code cleanly (10), test with edge cases (5).
How does the spaced re-solve rule work?
Re-solve a failed problem after 3 days, then after 7 days, without looking at the old solution. If you cannot reproduce it, the cycle repeats.
interview: You are stuck 15 minutes into a problem. What do you do?
Say so out loud, restate what the pattern should be, try the brute force to buy a working solution, and ask the interviewer a clarifying question — silence is the only wrong move.
How do you test your solution before telling the interviewer you are done?
Walk through the empty input, a single element, duplicates, and the boundary case, then trace one small example by hand and check the complexity aloud.
cards: Mock round
A timed 45-minute practice interview, talking aloud, with the same structure as the real thing.
Pattern-first reflex
Naming the pattern — two pointers, sliding window, BFS, DP — before writing any code.
Mistake log
A record of every failed or slow problem: pattern, what went wrong, and a re-solve date.
Spaced re-solve
Re-solving a failed problem after 3 days and again after 7 days, without peeking at the old solution.
Brute force first
Stating and coding the naive solution with its complexity before optimising — it anchors the discussion and banks partial credit.
Weekly Contest
LeetCode's Sunday timed contest: four problems under real pressure, the closest simulation of interview conditions.

D: I can analyse any solution's time and space complexity and pick the right pattern before coding.
I can solve unseen Medium problems with two pointers, sliding window, BFS/DFS and DP by recognising the pattern, not recalling a solution.
I can run a full 45-minute mock interview round — clarify, brute-force, optimise, code and test — and use my mistake log to re-solve failures after 3 and 7 days.
